Serious consumer delinquencies remain historically elevated in the US:

Student loan serious delinquencies rose +0.3 percentage points in Q2 2026, to 10.6%, the highest since Q1 2020.

This marks the 3rd consecutive quarterly increase, totaling +1.2 percentage points.

Credit card 90+ day delinquencies now stand at 12.9%, the 2nd-highest level since Q1 2011.

By comparison, credit card delinquencies peaked at 13.7% in Q2 2010, in the aftermath of the 2008 Financial Crisis.

Meanwhile, auto loan 90+ day delinquencies now stand at 5.5%, the 2nd-highest on record, surpassing the Q4 2010 high by 0.2 percentage points.

US consumers are struggling to keep up with their debt payments.

Yes, today's retail sales data was disappointing, but how bad is it out there for consumers?

Excellent dive into the data by @sonusvarghese right here. 

All in all? Things are still pretty good.

US consumers are extremely bullish on stocks:

The perceived probability among US consumers that US stock prices will be higher 1-year from now increased +0.5 percentage points in July, to 41.4%, the highest since April 2021.

Since March, this percentage has risen +5.1 points, marking the 2nd-highest reading since the 2020 pandemic.

By comparison, the April 2020 peak was 51.8%.

By age, consumers under 40 are the most optimistic, at 42.0%, the 2nd-highest since September 2024.

This is followed by the 40-59 age group, at 41.5%, the highest since January 2025, and consumers over 59, at 41.1%, the highest since September 2025.

Bullish sentiment is spreading across all consumer age groups.

The US job market is losing workers at an alarming pace:

The US labor force participation rate fell -0.1 percentage point in July, to 61.4%, the lowest since May 2020.

This metric measures the proportion of working-age Americans either employed or actively looking for work.

Excluding the 2020 pandemic, this is the lowest reading since March 1976.

The decrease also marks the 7th monthly decline over the last 8 months, bringing the cumulative drop to -1.1 percentage points.

This comes as -264,000 people left the labor force in July, following June's -720,000 decline, the 2nd-largest monthly decline since 2020.

Since November, the US labor force has shrunk by more than -2.4 million workers.

The US job market is much weaker under the surface than the headline data suggests.

With all the STRC doom loop FUD and people complaining about Saylor "forced selling" you'd expect MSTR investors to be more fearful than Bitcoiners right?

Nope.

Opposite actually.

This chart visualizes the fearful language of MSTR investors vs Bitcoiners.

It's interesting because it allows us to separate MSTR investor sentiment from the background emotional state of Bitcoin.

"But Sully, MSTR is a Bitcoin derivative, shouldn't the mood swings be more pronounced?"

This is often the case... but it's not the case right now.

There are a lot of potential reason for the widening psychological gap between investor bases (BIP-110, Coldard, etc). Regardless of the underlying reasons, the void is widening.

IMO this is one of the most fascinating dynamics in the space and basically no one is talking about it right now.
